fragments.text: Hello, I'm Tom Vaughn, Principal Engineer at the Common Crawl Foundation. I'll be speaking about why open data is essential for open models. Most of today's foundational AI models would not exist without open web data, but very few talk about the data that makes them possible. So what is Common Crawl? Common Crawl is a 501c3 non-profit organization that's been archiving the web since 2007. We've built a corpus of over 300 billion web pages. That's more than 10 petabytes of data. It's all free, open, and hosted on AWS S3 through their open web data sponsorship program. It's also heavily used. More than 10,000 research papers cite Common Crawl's data.

Every month we add between three and four billion new web pages to our archive. Our releases also include web graphs following each monthly crawl, from which we derive host-level and domain-level rankings, which steer our future crawls. We use harmonic centrality as a primary ranking algorithm, which is similar to page rank, but it's inherently harder to manipulate. This gives us a reliable way of seeing how well connected a host or domain is, allowing us to build a stratified sample of the web. This is harmonic centrality. In simple terms, the harmonic centrality of a vertex in a network measures how close that point is to all others. To find it, you look at every other point in the network,

measure the distance to each one, and then take the sum of the inverses of those distances. This means that points closer to many others have a higher harmonic centrality, while those further away from others have a lower one. You can see these rankings and compare them with page rank, and search through them on our website. At the domain level, we can search for Wikipedia here, and we'll see that it has a page rank position of 34 and a harmonic centrality position of 15. At the host level, we can search for Wikipedia, and we'll see the page rank and harmonic centrality positions for those hosts within that domain. So why is common crawl important? This is a cumulative plot of common crawl citations

in Google Scholar until January of 2025. You can see when the transformer paper was released in June of 2017. You can see when OpenAI released GPT-2 in February of 2019, and when big science bloom was released in July of 2022. For comparison, the Hubble Space Telescope is cited in a thousand papers per year. Common crawl is the backbone of modern AI. Over 80% of GPT-3's training tokens came from common crawl data. foundational data sets like Oscar, MC4, and the pile all rely on common crawl. So whenever you hear about a breakthrough in AI, the chances are it was fueled by open web data. There's a problem, however, with multi-lingual data. Our crawls contain much less content

in languages other than English. In fact, you can see that around 45% of the data was identified as English in our most recent crawl. The next biggest language represented is Russian with about 6% and then German with around 5.8%. The large trance you can see labeled other represents a long tail of low resource languages. That imbalance leads to risks. Research shows models often behave unsafely in low resource languages. GPT-PALN-2, LAMA-2, and VIKUNA give unsafe responses for queries in languages other than English. Imagine selling a car where the brakes and the seatbelts only work in English-speaking countries. No one would accept that. Yep, that's effectively what is happening with AI today.

One way forward is better language annotations. Our language annotations project is one way we're working on this. This initiative, which is hosted on ML Commons Dinerbench, aims to gather annotations for languages other than English. Another of our initiatives is our web languages project on GitHub, through which we gather URLs in as many languages as possible, which we then add to our seed crawl. The aim of these initiatives is to strengthen and celebrate language, community and culture. We need richer metadata, so researchers and developers know exactly what's in the dataset they're using. That transparency helps us spot gaps, improve representation, and helps model builders build safer multilingual systems. Without clarity on what's inside the data, we can't hope to fix

the problems downstream in the models. At the WMDQS or WIMDUX workshop at the column conference later this year in Montreal, and at similar forums, we're starting to see a global community form around these issues. People are realizing that data infrastructure is just as important as model architecture. It's not enough to scale compute and tweak parameters. We also need to invest in the pipelines, standards and transparency to keep AI safe and trustworthy. Open innovation depends on open foundations. The open source definition from the open source initiative has given us clear rules for software licensing. Rules that unlocked an entire ecosystem. We need something similar for AI data. Most datasets today don't come with those guarantees. Without open data, models aren't

truly open, and source code alone doesn't cut it. If you can't see the data, you can't reproduce the results, and you can't build real trust. There's also important work happening in signaling. Creative Commons has proposed CC signals, a way for creators to say how their work should or shouldn't be used in AI training. At the same time, working groups at the IETF are drafting standards for how websites can communicate with crawlers and automated agents. Beyond copyright debates, groups like OpenFuture argue that we should view generative AI as a cultural and social technology, one that changes how societies value and share knowledge. The point is that this isn't just a technical problem, it's a societal one. In conclusion, openness is more than access.

True openness requires licensing clarity, public infrastructure and shared standards, not just public URLs. Web scale data sets deserve web scale governance. We need common protocols for signaling, attribution and responsible reuse, like those emerging at Creative Commons and the IETF. We're building trust at the infrastructure layer, from licensing to language representation, common crawl enables transparency that model cards alone cannot provide. Openness must include everyone. If AI is to serve a global public, our data practices must reflect global voices, not just dominant languages or institutions. Open data is not a side issue, it's the foundation of AI. Without open transparent reproducible data, we cannot have open models. If we want AI that is safe, multilingual and genuinely innovative, we need to treat data infrastructure with the same

seriousness we give to models and compute. At common crawl, we're committed to that vision and we invite you to join us in making open data a global priority for AI. Thank you for listening. Please feel free to join us in our Discord server or in our Google group. You can scan the QR code to get access to these slides.
